content:
CIA Report of 1951 from Soviet journal Priroda titled Biochemical Resemblance Between Endoparasites and Malignant Tumors," written by Prof. V. V. Alpatov.

The report translates and condenses Alpatov's observations, noting that endoparasites (internal parasitic worms, especially intestinal ones) and malignant tumors (cancers) share striking biochemical and metabolic similarities due to the similar low-oxygen, hostile environments in which they grow and survive.

Main similarities highlighted:

Both exhibit pronounced anaerobic metabolism (relying on fermentation-like processes even when oxygen is limited).

They accumulate large amounts of glycogen (a stored carbohydrate) in their tissues.

Both are described as amphibolic (adaptable to both aerobic and anaerobic conditions), involving incomplete oxidations (aerobic under limited oxygen, but adapted to anaerobic states)

The article references earlier ideas (dating back long before 1950) suggesting tumors might have a "parasitic nature," though it focuses on metabolic parallels rather than claiming cancer is literally caused by parasites.

Specific Experiments and Compounds Mentioned

In 1938, H. Mauss synthesized Kyracyl D (an alkylated aminoxanthone), found effective against both bilharzia (schistosomiasis, a parasitic disease) and malignant tumors.

Guanazolo (also called Guanozolo; chemically 5-amino-7-hydroxy-1-v-triazolo[d]pyrimidine, or a guanine analog) suppresses nucleic acid synthesis in infusoria (protozoa) and in mice. It inhibits conversion of adenine to guanine and shows activity in malignant tumors with "dextrarotatory" (optically active) properties.

Alpatov, collaborating with O.K. Nastuykova, tested atebrin (also known as Atabrine or quinacrine, an antimalarial drug) and its optical enantiomorphs (mirror-image forms). They found that most test animals were more sensitive to the levorotatory form, but certain parasitic worms and tumors (e.g., Ehrlich's adenocarcinoma in mice, and intestinal parasites/nematodes in frogs) reacted oppositely to the optical forms of atebrin compared to healthy tissues. This helped distinguish parasitic worms and tumor tissues from normal ones.

I have always suspected a link between parasites and tumors, and this document further confirms that suspicion. But if we as humans have had such knowledge since 1938, the question is what we can do now.
